meta.title: Swahili B2 Upper Intermediate
meta.subtitle: 1500 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Swahili → English (see the Swahili, recall the meaning) and English → Swahili (see an English meaning, recall the Swahili). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 1500 words for an upper-intermediate learner, aligned to B2 of the Common European Framework of Reference, whose global descriptor begins 'Can understand the main ideas of complex text on both concrete and abstract topics, including technical discussions in his/her field of specialisation' — a learner here is able to interact with a degree of fluency and spontaneity that makes regular interaction with native speakers quite possible without strain for either party, and to produce clear, detailed text on a wide range of subjects and explain a viewpoint on a topical issue giving the advantages and disadvantages of various options. The words already taught by the levels below this one are left out. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: no exam board publishes a graded word list for Swahili that could be used here, so this deck is not any examination's vocabulary and does not claim to be. It is assembled from two things that can be stated. 261 of the 1500 come from a vocabulary written for the level's scope — the economy and business, government and politics, the law, rights, conflict and society, science and research, technology, the environment and geography, health and the body, education, literature, the arts and the media, home, family and possessions, character and feelings, arguing and analysing, the verbs of change and cause, describing, and the words that qualify and place a statement in time — and the other 1239 are the commonest remaining words, counted by the WHOLE word (every form of a noun, every conjugated form of a verb added together) in two collections of real Swahili, film and television subtitles and the Global Voices news site, a word having to be common in both. The cards are dealt by that frequency, so the words you meet most often come first. Verbs are shown as their infinitive (kusoma, to read) with their stem (-soma), which every tense is built on, and their negative infinitive; adjectives and possessives as their stem (-zuri, -angu) with the forms they take after three of the noun classes. The 1026 nouns show their class, which every adjective, verb and possessive agrees with, and their plural; there are 362 verbs. Real example sentences come with 497 of the 1500 words, three apiece for 110 of them, with the word picked out in colour and a speaker beside the sentence and the headword. Sources. Level: the Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe), global scale. Meanings, noun classes and forms: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency: counted from OpenSubtitles 2024 and Global Voices (CC BY 3.0), both as distributed by OPUS. Example sentences: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
